A soldier's love sounds sturdy, friend, but it isn't in the verse. The LORD says, “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride…” (Jeremiah 2:2). That's a wedding picture, not a barracks one. I'd have loved to see the soldier version, though, because it would come with a lot more saluting.

Close to the right neighborhood, but not the right house. The verse says, “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride…” (Jeremiah 2:2). A bride, friend, not a servant. Same devotion, very different picture.

It sounds reasonable, baker, but the verse says the opposite. Israel followed the LORD “…in the wilderness, in a land not sown.” (Jeremiah 2:2). Not sown means nobody had planted anything there. So no planted fields, just a long walk with Him.

That's right, friend. The LORD remembers how Israel followed Him “…in the wilderness, in a land not sown.” (Jeremiah 2:2). A land not sown means no planted fields at all. The question said planted fields, and the verse says the opposite.

That's it, baker. The verse says, “All who devoured her were found guilty; disaster came upon them…” (Jeremiah 2:3). The verse just before that calls Israel holy to the LORD. Anyone who went after her in those days ended up answering for it.

Nope, friend, nobody got promoted. The verse says, “All who devoured her were found guilty; disaster came upon them…” (Jeremiah 2:3). Being found guilty is a long way from being made her rulers. Disaster came upon them instead.

That would be a warm story, baker, but it's not this one. The verse says, “All who devoured her were found guilty; disaster came upon them…” (Jeremiah 2:3). Devouring Israel got them guilt and disaster. No invitation, no handshake, no cookie box.

explanations.answer: What fault they found in Him
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, friend. He asks, “What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me?” (Jeremiah 2:5). I think that question stings, because it asks them to name what went wrong. It's all about why they strayed from Him.

explanations.answer: Why they built so many cities
explanations.explanation: Cities never come up in this question, baker. The LORD asks, “What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me?” (Jeremiah 2:5). His focus is on why they strayed, not on any building projects. A construction crew couldn't answer this one for them.

explanations.answer: Where they hid all their gold
explanations.explanation: Gold never comes into it, friend. The LORD asks, “What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me?” (Jeremiah 2:5). He's asking why they drifted, not where the treasure went. No treasure map needed here.

That's the word, baker. “They followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves.” (Jeremiah 2:5). The fathers followed worthless idols first. After that, the verse says they became worthless themselves.

I wish that were the ending, friend, but it isn't. The verse says, “They followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves.” (Jeremiah 2:5). Powerful is nowhere in it. The word the LORD uses is worthless.

Holy is a good word, baker, but not the one here. Israel was once holy to the LORD (Jeremiah 2:3), but the fathers who followed idols “…became worthless themselves.” (Jeremiah 2:5). The verse says they followed the idols and then became worthless. Holy was where they started, and worthless is where the idols left them.

explanations.answer: Where is the LORD who brought us out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says they did not ask, “Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt…” (Jeremiah 2:6). He had led them through the wilderness, and still they did not ask where He was. I think that missing question is what makes His words sting.

explanations.answer: Why did we ever leave the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the verse, friend. What they did not ask was, “Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt…” (Jeremiah 2:6). The verse is about the LORD who brought them out, not a complaint about leaving. The missing question was about Him.

explanations.answer: Who will give us a king like the nations
explanations.explanation: No king question here, baker. The verse says they did not ask, “Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt…” (Jeremiah 2:6). The one they did not ask about was the LORD Himself. Nobody was shopping for a king in this verse.

I wish that were true, friend, but the LORD says otherwise. “I brought you into a fertile land to eat its fruit and bounty, but you came and defiled My land and made My inheritance detestable.” (Jeremiah 2:7). He brought them into a good land, and they defiled it instead. So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “…you came and defiled My land and made My inheritance detestable.” (Jeremiah 2:7). He had brought them into a fertile land, and they defiled it. So they did not keep it holy.

That's right, friend. The verse says, “The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed useless idols.” (Jeremiah 2:8). Baal was a false god, and the prophets spoke in his name. So the priests, the leaders and the prophets all turned from the LORD.

Sadly, the prophets are on the list too, baker. The text says, “The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed useless idols.” (Jeremiah 2:8). Baal was a false god. The priests, the experts in the law, the leaders and the prophets are all named in that one verse.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “Therefore, I will contend with you again, declares the LORD, and I will bring a case against your children’s children.” (Jeremiah 2:9). His case reaches past the people standing there. It reaches down to their children's children.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says He will “…bring a case against your children’s children.” (Jeremiah 2:9). So His case isn't only about the people living right then. It reaches to the generations after them too.

That's the one, baker. The LORD asks, “Has a nation ever changed its gods?” (Jeremiah 2:11). He sends them out to look at the coasts of Cyprus and to Kedar, and to see if anything like this has happened. Even people with gods that aren't gods at all stay loyal to them.

No shepherd or crown in this one, friend. The question is, “Has a nation ever changed its gods?” (Jeremiah 2:11). That's what the LORD wants them to go and look into. Nobody's getting crowned in these verses.

Temple building isn't what's being asked, baker. The LORD asks, “Has a nation ever changed its gods?” (Jeremiah 2:11). The whole point is about swapping gods, not putting up a building. Just a swap, and a shocking one.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “…My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols.” (Jeremiah 2:11). They gave up their Glory and took idols the verse calls useless. That's a trade nobody should want.

Horses never show up in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “…My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols.” (Jeremiah 2:11). What they got in the trade was idols, and the idols were useless. No horses, just a very bad swap.

Gold would at least look shiny, friend, but it isn't the answer. The LORD says, “…My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols.” (Jeremiah 2:11). They gave up the Glory and took useless idols. That's about as bad a trade as handing over a fresh cookie box and getting back an empty tray.

That would be the opposite, baker. The LORD says, “Be stunned by this, O heavens; be shocked and utterly appalled…” (Jeremiah 2:12). The heavens aren't called to sing, they're called to be stunned. There's no joyful tune in this verse.
That's right, friend. He tells the heavens, “Be stunned by this, O heavens; be shocked and utterly appalled…” (Jeremiah 2:12). Singing for joy isn't in the verse. Being shocked is.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water…” (Jeremiah 2:13). A fountain keeps flowing, and that's what they walked away from. Walking away from a fountain is a strange way to handle being thirsty.

The rock of their salvation sounds lovely, friend, but it isn't what this verse says. Here He says, “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water…” (Jeremiah 2:13). Stay with the verse in front of you. In this one, He's the fountain.

The shepherd is a good picture, baker, but not this verse's picture. The LORD says, “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water…” (Jeremiah 2:13). Here the image is water that keeps flowing. Nobody's herding anything in this one.

I'd love that to be true, friend, but the verse says otherwise. They dug “…broken cisterns that cannot hold water.” (Jeremiah 2:13). A cistern that can't hold water isn't much of a cistern. It's a hole with ambition.

Correct, baker. The LORD calls them “…broken cisterns that cannot hold water.” (Jeremiah 2:13). They dug these themselves, and they don't work. Same as me trying to bake with a stamper that has no edges left, which gives you a smudge and a sad face.

You've got it, friend. The LORD says, “The young lions have roared at him; they have sounded their voices.” (Jeremiah 2:15). Israel has become prey, and the lions are the ones roaring. I think this is a heavy picture.

Bulls make a lot of noise, baker, but they're not in this verse. The text says, “The young lions have roared at him; they have sounded their voices.” (Jeremiah 2:15). The roaring comes from young lions. Bulls don't get a line here.

Jackals aren't in the verse, friend. The text says, “The young lions have roared at him; they have sounded their voices.” (Jeremiah 2:15). Prey meets lions here, and that's the picture. I'd keep the jackals out of it.

Not quite, baker. The verse says the young lions “…have laid waste his land; his cities lie in ruins, without inhabitant.” (Jeremiah 2:15). Without inhabitant means nobody is living there. Those cities are empty, not full.
That's right, friend. The verse says, “his cities lie in ruins, without inhabitant.” (Jeremiah 2:15). Nobody is living in them. A town like that doesn't have a single person to wave at you.

That's the pointed one, baker. The LORD asks, “Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?” (Jeremiah 2:17). He asks whether Israel brought this on himself by forsaking Him. The question points right back at Israel.

Kedar was just a place the LORD named earlier, friend. He sent them to look there to see if anything like this had ever happened (Jeremiah 2:10). Then He asks, “Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?” (Jeremiah 2:17). So the answer points back at Israel, not at Kedar.

Cyprus was just one of the places the LORD told them to look at, baker (Jeremiah 2:10). He wasn't pointing a finger there. The question is, “Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?” (Jeremiah 2:17). The finger turns back to Israel himself.

That's the river, friend. The LORD asks, “…what will you gain on your way to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile?” (Jeremiah 2:18). He asks the same thing about the Euphrates on the way to Assyria. Two roads, two rivers, and one question about what Israel gains.

Good river, baker, but I'd stick to the map in this verse. The LORD asks, “…what will you gain on your way to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile?” (Jeremiah 2:18). The Nile goes with Egypt, and the Euphrates goes with Assyria in the next question. The Jordan will have to sit this one out.

Jabbok isn't in this verse, friend. The LORD asks, “…what will you gain on your way to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile?” (Jeremiah 2:18). The river for Egypt is the Nile. The next line brings in the Euphrates for Assyria.

That's right, baker. The Lord GOD of Hosts says, “Consider and realize how evil and bitter it is for you to forsake the LORD your God and to have no fear of Me…” (Jeremiah 2:19). He wants them to stop and really think about it. Sometimes you need to look at what you've done with both eyes open.

It really is in there, friend. The Lord GOD of Hosts says, “Consider and realize how evil and bitter it is for you to forsake the LORD your God and to have no fear of Me…” (Jeremiah 2:19). Evil and bitter are the two words He picks, and He asks them to stop and think it over, so the statement is true. I get it, though.
